ety: From Middle English bothe, boþe, from Old English bā þā (“both the; both those”) and possibly reinforced by Old Norse báðir, from Proto-Germanic *bai. Cognate with Saterland Frisian bee (“both”), West Frisian beide (“both”), Dutch beide (“both”), German beide (“both”), Swedish både, båda, Danish både, Norwegian både, Icelandic báðir. Replaced Middle English bō, from Old English bā, a form of Old English bēġen. A remnant of the Indo-European dual grammatical number.

s.def: Each of the two; one and the other; referring to two individuals or items.
ex: Both (the/my) children are such dolls.
Which one do you need? ―I need both of them.
He will not bear the loss of his rank, because he can bear the loss of his estate; but he will bear both, because he is prepared for both.

s.def: Each of the two, or of the two kinds.
ex: Did you want this one or that one? ―Give me both.
They were both here.
I've already lost both (of) my parents.

s.def: both...and...
Including both of (used with and).
ex: I (can) both sing and dance.
Both you and I are students.
Mind you, clothes were clothes in those days. There was a great deal of them, lavish both in material and in workmanship.

s.def: Including all of (used with and).
ex: […] having much aduantage both in number, valure, and forepreparation […]
Both mongrel, puppy, whelp, and hound.
He prayeth well who loveth well both man and bird and beast.

ety: Borrowed from Scots bauther, bather (“to bother”). Origin unknown. Perhaps related to Scots pother (“to make a stir or commotion, bustle”), also of unknown origin. Compare English pother (“to poke, prod”), variant of potter (“to poke”). More at potter. Perhaps related to Irish bodhaire (“noise”), Irish bodhraim (“to deafen, annoy”).

s.def: To annoy, to disturb, to irritate; to be troublesome to, to make trouble for.
ex: Would it bother you if I smoked?

s.def: To take the trouble, to trouble oneself (to do something).
ex: Why do I even bother to try?

s.def: to take the trouble, to trouble oneself to do something
To feel care or concern; to burden or inconvenience oneself out of concern.
ex: I never bother about such trivialities.
I wouldn't bother with an umbrella if I were you.

s.def: Fuss, ado.
ex: There was a bit of bother at the hairdresser's when they couldn't find my appointment in the book.
It was a 15-minute return trip to walk back home to pick up my device, but I weighed it up and decided that it wasn’t worth the bother.

s.def: Trouble, inconvenience.
ex: Yes, I can do that for you—it’s no bother.

s.def: A mild expression of annoyance.
ex: "Oh, help!" said Pooh. "I'd better go back." "Oh, bother!" said Pooh. "I shall have to go on." "I can't do either!" said Pooh. "Oh, help and bother!"

ety: From bother + -ation (suffix indicating an action or process, or its result).

s.def: A mild expression of annoyance or exasperation: bother!
ex: "Botheration ! Who cares ? Why don't you ask if [our ancestors] carried pocket-books ?"
Botheration! How she had crumpled her skirt, kneeling in that idiotic way.
"Blast and botheration!" exclaimed Digory. "What's gone wrong now? [...]"

s.def: The state of being bothered; annoyance, vexation.
ex: [...] I am determined to be peevish after my long day's botheration.
At home he read too many papers. He was better off without his daily dose of world botheration, sham happenings, without newspaper phrases.

s.def: An act of bothering or annoying.
A person or thing that causes bother, inconvenience, trouble, etc.

ety: Probably from booth + -y (diminutive suffix). Booth is ultimately derived from Proto-Germanic *bōþō (“building; dwelling; hut”), from *būaną (“to dwell, reside”), possibly from Proto-Indo-European *bʰuH- (“to be”). The short vowel /ɒ/, /ɑ/, etc., in the first syllable instead of the long vowel /uː/ in booth may be due to the influence of Irish both and Scottish Gaelic both (“booth, hut”), which have the same etymology as booth.

s.def: A small cottage or hut; specifically (Scotland), one often left unlocked for communal use in a remote, often mountainous, area by hikers, labourers, etc.
ex: Often Neil sat in their bothy on winter nights and told Calum about seas he had never seen.
The Bog Creeper came out her wee bothy so I stood on the toilet seat and Lanna whipped her skirt down to her boots and sat.
It was easy then to meet with a man / shifting himself to a safer distance / to bed in the bothies[.]

s.def: A building for workers to rest in.
A building on a farm, sometimes with just one room, for (usually unmarried male) farmworkers or other labourers to live in.

ety: Blend of botulinum + toxin.

s.def: A toxic compound (generic name botulinum toxin type A) produced by the bacterium Clostridium botulinum, that causes the paralysis of muscles, used in cosmetic surgery to conceal wrinkles and for muscle spasm relief and headache prevention.
ex: Eric Andre: You look phenomenal. What's your secret? Asa Akira: Botox. Eric Andre: Really? Asa Akira: Yeah. And I'm starving.

ety: Etymology tree Proto-Bantu *bʊ̀- Tswana bo- Tswana Tswana Tswana Botswanabor. English Botswana Borrowed from Tswana Botswana, from bo- + Tswana, of uncertain origin.

s.def: A country in Southern Africa. Capital: Gaborone.
ex: After independence, Rhodesia changed its name to Zimbabwe, Nyasaland to Malawi, and Bechuanaland to Botswana.
According to Masisi, Botswana has seen its elephant population grow to some 130,000.

ety: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *bʰeHw-der. Ancient Greekbor.? Latin buttis Proto-Indo-European *-lós Proto-Indo-European *-elós Proto-Italic *-elos Proto-Italic *-kelos Latin -culus Late Latin butticula Old French boteillebor. Middle English botel English bottle From Middle English botel (“bottle, flask, wineskin”), from Old French boteille, from Late Latin butticula, diminutive of buttis (“cask”). Doublet of botija. Displaced native pinne and non-native Old English ampella. Partially displ…

s.def: The contents of such a container.
ex: I only drank a bottle of beer.

s.def: container
To seal (a liquid) into a bottle for later consumption. Also fig.
ex: This plant bottles vast quantities of spring water every day.

s.def: A container, typically made of glass or plastic and having a tapered neck, used primarily for holding liquids.
ex: Beer is often sold in bottles.
Jack and Gill Went up the hill, To fetch a bottle of water.

s.def: A container with a rubber nipple used for giving liquids to infants, a baby bottle.
ex: The baby wants a bottle.
With Marvin getting older ... and walking now ... I thought it was time to start weaning him off of his bottle.

s.def: (originally bottle and glass as rhyming slang for "arse") Nerve, courage.
ex: You don’t have the bottle to do that!
He was going to ask her out, but he lost his bottle when he saw her.
He told me I didn’t have the bottle to take them, so I told him I did and he handed them to me one by one and I swallowed them.

s.def: A container of hair dye, hence with one’s hair color produced by dyeing.
ex: Did you know he’s a bottle brunette? His natural hair color is strawberry blonde.

s.def: Intoxicating liquor; alcohol.
ex: to drown one’s troubles in the bottle
to hit the bottle
See, my old man’s got a problem / He live with the bottle, that’s the way it is

s.def: To feed (an infant) baby formula.
ex: Because of complications she can't breast feed her baby and so she bottles him.

s.def: To refrain from doing (something) at the last moment because of a sudden loss of courage.
ex: The rider bottled the big jump.

s.def: device to open bottles removing the cap
A device used to remove the cap from a bottle.
A device used to remove the cork from a bottle.

ety: From bottle + brush.

s.def: A cylindrical brush on a thin shaft that is used to clean bottles.

Any of various trees or shrubs of the myrtle family, especially of the genera Callistemon and Melaleuca, native to Australia and adjacent areas, having spikes of flowers with numerous conspicuous stamens.
ex: ‘But look, there's some grass up till this bottlebrush which looks like it's bin trampled.’

s.def: An uncommon cave formation resulting from a rise in water level such that a stalactite becomes immersed in water that is supersaturated with calcium carbonate, causing the stalactite to become coated with pool spar.
Drinking water sold by bottle, either natural or processed by e.g. filtering, carbonation or mineralization.

ety: From bottle + fish.

s.def: blowfish

ety: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *bʰeHw-der. Ancient Greekbor.? Latin buttis Proto-Indo-European *-lós Proto-Indo-European *-elós Proto-Italic *-elos Proto-Italic *-kelos Latin -culus Late Latin butticula Old French boteillebor. Middle English botel English bottle Proto-Germanic *hnakkô Proto-West Germanic *hnakkō Old English hnecca Middle English nekke English neck English bottleneck From bottle + neck.

s.def: The narrow portion that forms the pouring spout of a bottle; the neck of a bottle.
In traffic, any narrowing of the road, especially resulting in a delay.
The part of a process that is too slow or cumbersome due to the lessening of available throughput.
ex: It is easy to create entries; processing the paperwork is the bottleneck.
The bottleneck in this computer program is the inefficient sorting process; we should replace it with a faster one.

s.def: To slow by causing a bottleneck.
ex: The merge bottlenecked the traffic every morning.

s.def: To form a bottleneck.
ex: The traffic bottlenecked at the merge every morning.

ety: From bottle + nose. The creatures have a bottle-shaped nose.

s.def: bottlenose dolphin.
bottlenose whale.
bottlenose skate.
The beak or rostrum of a dolphin.
ex: The dolphin’s bottlenose struck the boy causing fatal internal injuries.

s.def: species of dolphin
One of the species of gray dolphin in the genus Tursiops, between two and four meters in length, inhabiting warm and temperate seas worldwide.

ety: PIE word *bʰudʰmḗn Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *dʰewbʰ-? Proto-Indo-European *-mḗn Proto-Indo-European *bʰudʰmḗn Proto-Germanic *butmaz Proto-West Germanic *botm Old English botm Middle English botme English bottom From Middle English botme, botom, from Old English botm, bodan (“bottom, foundation; ground, abyss”), from Proto-West Germanic *butm, from Proto-Germanic *butmaz, *budmaz (“bottom; ground”), from Proto-Indo-European *bʰudʰmḗn (“bottom”). Cognates Cognate with Yola bothom, bott…

s.def: lowest part
slang: penetrated partner in sex
The lowest part of anything.
ex: barrels with the bottoms knocked out
a great ship’s kettle of iron, with the bottom knocked out
At the bottom of the staircase I stood and stared at the worn steps, and Ayesha, turning, saw me.

s.def: The remotest or innermost part of something.
ex: Near-synonym: fundus (anatomical)
There’s a fairy at the bottom of my garden.
I walked to the bottom of the street.

s.def: The fundamental part; a basic aspect.
ex: get to the bottom of it

s.def: Low-lying land; a valley or hollow.
ex: Where shall we go for a walk? How about Ashcombe Bottom?
The horses staled in a small brook that runs in a bottom, betwixt two hills.
the bottoms and the high grounds

s.def: Low-lying land near a river with alluvial soil.
The buttocks or anus.
ex: Calvin, if you shoot that paper clip at me, I'll get your bottom hauled to the principal's office so fast you'll think you were in a time warp!!

s.def: The bed of a body of water.
An abyss.
ex: In the Carpathian Bottom makes abode / The Shepherd of the Seas, a Prophet and a God

der: ambulance at the bottom of a cliff
at the bottom of the pile

s.def: bottom quark
A quark having a fractional electric charge of -1/3 and a mass of about 4,100 to 4,400 MeV.
A quark having a fractional electric charge of -1/3 and a mass of about 4,100 to 4,400 MeV. Symbol: b

ety: From Middle English botemles, botmeles, equivalent to bottom + -less. Cognate with West Frisian boaiemleas (“bottomless”), Dutch bodemloos (“bottomless”), German Low German boddenloos (“bottomless”), German bodenlos (“bottomless”), Swedish bottenlös (“bottomless”), Icelandic botnlaus (“bottomless”).

s.def: Having no bottom.
ex: And while the railway's finances will forever remain a bottomless black hole, Highways England finances are rapidly becoming a bottomless pothole!

s.def: Extremely deep.
Having no bounds; limitless.
ex: The restaurant offered bottomless drinks.

s.def: Of a meal: accompanied by unlimited drinks.
ex: I get a message from some school friends about a bottomless brunch they want to go to.

s.def: Difficult to understand; unfathomable.
refillable (usually for iced tea or other such cold beverages)
Not wearing clothes below the waist; particularly not wearing clothes that would cover the genitalia.

ety: From Revelation 9:1–12.

s.def: A pit with no visible bottom and apparently infinite depth.
Hell.
An endless resource or supply.
A person with an apparently boundless appetite; an entity or problem which consumes seemingly endless resources.
An in-game hazard made up of a deep hole or void with no visible bottom, falling into which typically costs the player a life.

ety: An allusion to the bottoms of the drinkers' glasses being raised.

s.def: Cheers! (the drinking toast)

ety: From German Botulin, from Latin botulus (“sausage”).

s.def: An extremely potent nerve toxin produced by the anaerobic bacteria Clostridium botulinum. Ingesting botulin results in the serious medical condition of botulism.

ety: From German Botulismus, from Latin botulus (“sausage”), the first identified source of the disease, + -ism.

s.def: Poisoning caused by the toxin from Clostridium botulinum, an anaerobic bacterium that grows in improperly prepared food.
Alternative spelling of bouclé.

ety: Borrowed from French boudoir, from bouder (“to sulk”), of Germanic origin.

s.def: A woman's private sitting room, dressing room, or bedroom.
ex: The Duchesse's boudoir was fitted up in a style of luxury utterly different from anything before familiar to the Carraras.
I found her in her boudoir getting outside a dish of tea and a crumpet.

s.def: An army tent.

ety: From French bouffant, from Middle French; present participle of bouffer (“to puff”). Doublet of buffont.

s.def: Of hair or clothing, full-bodied or puffy; puffed out away from head or body.
ex: Her bouffant suit made her seem much heavier than her petite figure actually was.

s.def: A puffy, round hairstyle, popular in the mid-to-late 16th century, characterized by hair raised high on the head and usually covering the ears or hanging down on the sides.
ex: Mother went a little pale. “Preposterous!” she said. “I don’t know what’s got into you!” She fiddled with her bouffant, almost as if she was nervous.

ety: From taxonomic name Bougainvillea, from French Bougainville + -a. Named after French admiral and explorer Louis Antoine de Bougainville (1729–1811).

s.def: Any of several South American flowering shrubs or lianas, of the genus Bougainvillea, having three showy, colorful bracts attached below each group of three inconspicuous flowers.
ex: He arrives bearing flowers as though he's come to court me. Tonight he brings me bougainvillea. It is always a surprise.
He is outside in his garden, surrounded by bougainvillea bursting with color.

ety: PIE word *bʰeh₂ǵʰús From Middle English bough (“branch of a bush or tree, especially a main branch; limb of an animal or person; something resembling a branch (such as a plant root or branch of a nerve); (figuratively) Christian cross; descendant, offspring”) [and other forms], from Old English bōg, bōh (“tree bough or branch; arm; shoulder”), from Proto-West Germanic *bōgu, from Proto-Germanic *bōguz (“shoulder; upper arm”), from Proto-Indo-European *bʰeh₂ǵʰús (“arm”). Cognate with Saterland F…

s.def: A tree-branch, usually a primary one directly attached to the trunk.
ex: When the bough breaks, the cradle will fall. (Rock-a-bye Baby)
Ah, happy, happy boughs! that cannot shed / Your leaves, nor ever bid the Spring adieu; […]
A pair of birds settle on the bough above them, murmuring together, ready to roost.

s.def: A gallows.

ety: Borrowed from French bougie (“wax candle”), after the Algerian city Bougie (Béjaïa), and the tapered, hand-dipped candles it made. The medical instruments were originally made from waxed linen. Doublet of bugia.

s.def: A tapered cylindrical instrument for introducing an object into a tubular anatomical structure, or to dilate such a structure, as with an esophageal bougie.
A wax candle.
Behaving like or pertaining to people of a higher social status, middle-class / bourgeois people (sometimes carrying connotations of fakeness, elitism, or snobbery).
ex: Hey, look, man, I haven't changed, I'm not gonna change and I'm not down with this bougie stuff.
I'll be on the movie screens / Magazines and bougie scenes
Shangela is kind of bougie, but she's also your homegirl.

s.def: Fancy or good-looking, without connotations of snobbery or pretentiousness.
A person who exhibits bougie behavior.
Alternative spelling of bowjy (“shed for cattle or sheep”).

ety: Borrowed from French bouillabaisse, from Occitan bolhabaissa, bouiabaisso, possibly a compound of bolhir (“to boil”) + abaissar (“to lower (the temperature)”).

s.def: A type of fish soup or stew from Provence, France.
A chaotic, disorganized mixture; a confused hodgepodge.

ety: First attested 1656, from French bouillon, from the verb bouillir (“to boil”), from Old French boillir, from Latin bullīre (“to bubble, boil”), from bulla (“bubble”).

s.def: A clear seasoned broth made by simmering usually light meat, such as beef or chicken.
An excrescence on a horse's frush or frog.

ety: From late Middle English bulder, short for Middle English bulder ston (“a stone that's been worn into a round shape, boulder, cobblestone”), possibly from Old Swedish *buldersten, itself possibly from Old Swedish bulder (“rumble, noise”) + sten (“stone”); whence dialectal Swedish bullersten (“large stone in a stream, causing water to roar around it”). The first element may alternatively be allied to Old Swedish bulle, bolle (“round drinking vessel, tumbler”), from Old Norse bolli, related to Ol…

s.def: A large mass of stone detached from the surrounding land.
A particle greater than 256 mm in diameter, following the Wentworth scale
A large marble, in children's games.
ex: There were four sizes of marbles and we called them boulders, biggies, regulars, and teenies.

s.def: A session of bouldering; involvement in bouldering.

ety: Borrowed from French boulevard, from Middle French boulevard, bollevart, boulevars, bolevers, bollewerc (“rampart”), from Middle High German bolewerc, bolwerc (modern German Bollwerk) or Middle Dutch bolwerk (“bulwark, bastion”). Doublet of bulwark; more at bole, work.

s.def: A broad, well-paved and landscaped thoroughfare.
ex: We live on Sunset Boulevard.

s.def: The landscaping on the sides of a boulevard or other thoroughfare.
A strip of land between a street and sidewalk.
The grassy area in the middle of some streets; a refuge island.

ety: From Middle English bounsen, bunsen (“to beat, thump”), cognate with Scots bunce, bonce (“to bounce”). Of uncertain origin. Perhaps imitative, related to bump, or related to Middle English bonchen (“to pound, beat”) and Dutch bonken (“to bump”). Compare Saterland Frisian bumzje (“to pound, bang, bounce”), West Frisian bûnzje (“to throb, bounce, pulsate”), Dutch bonzen (“to thump, knock, throb, bounce”), German Low German bunsen, bumsen (“to beat, bounce”), German bumsen (“to thud, bang, pound”).

s.def: To change the direction of motion after hitting an obstacle.
ex: The tennis ball bounced off the wall before coming to rest in the ditch.

s.def: To move quickly up and then down (or vice versa), once or repeatedly.
ex: He bounces nervously on his chair.

s.def: To cause to move quickly up and down, or back and forth, once or repeatedly.
ex: He bounced the child on his knee.
The children were bouncing a ball against a wall.

s.def: To suggest or introduce (an idea, etc.) to (off or by) someone, in order to gain feedback.
ex: I'm meeting Bob later to bounce some ideas off him about the new product range.

s.def: To leap or spring suddenly or unceremoniously; to bound.
ex: She bounced happily into the room.
Out bounced the mastiff.

s.def: To move rapidly (between).
To be refused by a bank because it is drawn on insufficient funds.
ex: We can’t accept further checks from you, as your last one bounced.

s.def: To fail to cover (have sufficient funds for) (a cheque/check drawn on one's account).
ex: He tends to bounce a check or two toward the end of each month, before his payday.

s.def: To leave.
ex: Let’s wrap this up, I gotta bounce.

s.def: To eject violently, as from a room; to discharge unceremoniously, as from employment.
ex: Nobody took umbrage and bounced me out of the Union for being a pro.
Anyone who gets bounced out of [this bar] is not just pushed onto the street — he is walked home, or put in a cab.

ety: Etymology tree English bounce Proto-Indo-European *-yósder. Proto-Italic *-āzios Latin -āriusnom. Latin -āriusbor. Proto-Germanic *-ārijaz Proto-West Germanic *-ārī Old English -ere Middle English -ere English -er English bouncer From bounce + -er.

s.def: A person or thing that bounces something, such as a ball.
A member of security personnel employed by bars, nightclubs, etc. to decide who can enter, maintain order, and deal with patrons who cause trouble.
ex: At 199 centimetres and a hundred kilos going up, he was scary big and he found work as a bouncer and enforcer[.]

s.def: A short-pitched ball that bounces up towards, or above the height of the batsman’s head.
ex: ‘You try to hit the bouncer that you should duck under. Your bat misses it completely. The ball strikes your temple, whack!’

s.def: An account or server (as with IRC and FTP) that invisibly redirects requests to another, used for anonymity or vanity.
One who bounces; a large, heavy person who makes much noise in moving.
A boaster; a bully.
Something big; a good stout example of the kind.
ex: The stone must be a bouncer.

s.def: A bold lie.
ex: "… when he wants to accomplish his purpose, he does not hesitate to invent—I am not quite sure of the word, but I think it is “bouncers.”

s.def: A liar.
A bouncy castle.
A large inflatable structure, resembling a castle etc., on which children jump and play as on a trampoline.

ety: From Middle English bound, bund (preterite) and bounden, bunden, ibunden, ȝebunden (past participle), from Old English bund- and bunden, ġebunden respectively. See bind.

s.def: simple past and past participle of bind
ex: I bound the splint to my leg.
I had bound the splint with duct tape.

s.def: Obliged (to).
ex: You are not legally bound to reply.
Well, it isn't for me to say. I'm an employee of the firm and bound to stand by it.

s.def: That cannot stand alone as a free word.
Constrained by a quantifier.
Constipated; costive.
Confined or restricted to a certain place.
Unable to move in certain conditions.
Ready, prepared.
ex: This certain,—that a band of war / Has for two days been ready boune, / At prompt command to march from Doune […].

s.def: Ready to start or go (to); moving in the direction (of).
ex: Which way are you bound? —I'm already homeward bound.
Is that message bound for me?
When she is depressed she hops in a taxi cab bound nowhere special and falls apart against the Naugahyde.

s.def: Very likely (to), certain to
ex: They were bound to come into conflict eventually.
Don’t go around tonight— / Well, it’s bound to take your life: / There’s a bad moon on the rise.

ety: Analogous to bound morpheme, compound of bound and termineme.

s.def: (terminology) A termineme that cannot stand alone in its related domain or environment, a terminological bound morpheme.

ety: Etymology tree English bound Proto-Indo-European *-yósder. Proto-Italic *-āzios Latin -āriusder. Middle English -arie English -ary English boundary From bound + -ary. Semantically displaced native Old English mearc (“boundary, limit”) whence Modern English mark.

s.def: The dividing line or location between two areas.
The bounds, confines, or limits between immaterial things (such as one’s comfort zone, privacy, or professional sphere and the realm beyond).
ex: I didn’t mean to push the boundaries by sending my boss a message on Saturday night.

s.def: An edge or line marking an edge of the playing field.

An event whereby the ball is struck and either touches or passes over a boundary (with or without bouncing), usually resulting in an award of 4 (four) or 6 (six) runs respectively for the batting team.
ex: Travis hit a boundary to seal the match on the last ball of the over.

s.def: (of a set) The set of points in the closure of a set S, not belonging to the interior of that set.
Commission paid by a bus or jeepney driver to a public transportation operator for taking passengers, or the excess collected fares taken as daily wage.
Any function whose values remain bounded by some constant.

ety: From bound + -en, the archaic past participle of bind.

s.def: Now chiefly in "bounden duty": made obligatory; binding.
ex: That I wad wi' a' my heart; and mickle obliged to your honour for putting me in mind o' my bounden duty.

s.def: Bound.
ex: ...and that the world should owe thanke therof to you, to whom my husband the authour of it was for good receyued of you, most dutiefully bounden.

s.def: past participle of bind.
ex: He'll mind, I reckon, not getting any work out'n me, but I won't be bounden to him any longer. How can he keep me if I ain't bounden to him?

ety: From bound + -er. Sense 2 poss. from bandar, borrowed from Hindi बन्दर (bandar, “monkey”), via Indian English.

s.def: Something that bounds or jumps.
A dishonourable man; a cad.
ex: He marvelled anew that Ruth could have cared, as she certainly had, for this fellow. A bounder, and worse than a bounder.

s.def: A social climber.
That which limits; a boundary.
A four-wheeled type of dogcart or cabriolet.

ety: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *bʰuH- Proto-Germanic *būaną Old Norse búinnbor. Middle English bownde English bound Proto-Indo-European *lewh₁- Proto-Indo-European *lewHs-der. Proto-Germanic *leusaną Proto-Germanic *lausaz Proto-Germanic *-lausaz Proto-West Germanic *-laus Old English -lēas Middle English -les English -less English boundless From bound + -less.

s.def: Without bounds, unbounded.
ex: Round the decay / Of that colossal wreck, boundless and bare / The lone and level sands stretch far away.

ety: Inherited from Middle English bountevous, from Old French bontios; by surface analysis, bounty + ous.

s.def: Inclined to be generous.
ex: Which with a bounteous hand was kindly lent

s.def: Liberal or abundant.
ex: “I’d like to say it’s not just bounteous privilege, but it is. People like Boris Johnson, Rishi Sunak, they’re incredibly cut off from the world. […]

s.def: Large.
ex: The house came with a bounteous yard.
He was a big man with a bounteous belly.

ety: From bounty + -ful.

s.def: Having a quantity or amount that is generous or plentiful; ample.
ex: They enjoyed a wet summer and a bountiful harvest.
The vile person shall be no more called liberal, nor the churl said to be bountiful.

ety: From Middle English bounte (“goodness, virtue; beauty; strength; chivalry, valour; excellence; kindness, mercy; good deed; generosity”) [and other forms], borrowed from Anglo-Norman bounté and Old French bonté, bontet, bunté (modern French bonté (“goodness, kindness”)), from Latin bonitās.

s.def: Something given liberally; a gift.

ety: From Middle English bredthe, alteration (due to nouns ending in -th: length, strength, wrength, etc.) of brede ("breadth"; see bread). Equivalent to broad + -th (abstract nominal suffix). Cognate with Scots bredth (“breadth”), Saterland Frisian Bratte (“breadth”), West Frisian breedte (“breadth”), Dutch breedte (“breadth”), German Low German Breddte, Breddt (“breadth”), German Breite (“breadth”), Danish bredde (“breadth”), Norwegian Bokmål bredde (“breadth”), Swedish bredd (“breadth”).

ety: Unknown; many unproven and widely debated theories exist. ety: Inherited from Middle English breken bred; under medieval conditions, guests brought their own knives worn with them, which were their daggers they hunted and gathered with, then only fit to cut meat. News that has either just happened or is currently happening.

Any major progress; such as a great innovation or discovery that overcomes a significant obstacle.

ety: From break + water. Compare Dutch breekwater (“breakwater”). Compare firebreak.

s.def: A species in that genus, Abramis brama.
A European fresh-water cyprinoid fish of the genus Abramis, little valued as food. Several species are known.
An American fresh-water fish, of various species of Lepomis and allied genera, which are also called sunfishes and pondfishes.
A marine sparoid fish of the genus Pagellus, and allied genera.
To clean (e.g. a ship's bottom of clinging shells, seaweed, etc.) by the application of fire and scraping.

s.def: A person who purchases items for resale in a retail establishment.
ex: The supermarket's new buyer decided to stock a larger range of vegetarian foods.

s.def: A person who purchases items consumed or used as components in the manufacture of products.

ety: From Middle English *bussen (suggested by Middle English bussyng (“buzzing”)), of onomatopoeic origin. Cognate with Scots bizz (“to buzz”). Compare Middle English bunning (“buzzing”), Middle English hossing (“buzzing”), Middle English bissen (“to hush”).

s.def: A continuous humming noise, as of bees; a confused murmur, as of general conversation in low tones.
ex: In the steady buzz of flies the homeward-bound agent was lying flushed and insensible[.]

s.def: The audible friction of voiced consonants.
A rush or feeling of energy or excitement; a feeling of slight intoxication.
ex: Still feeling the buzz from the coffee, he pushed through the last of the homework.

s.def: A telephone call or e-mail.
ex: Now, don't waste time, give us a buzz -- quick! 825-4703 or 265-7881.

s.def: Major topic of conversation; widespread rumor; information spread behind the scenes.
ex: Mr. Hall? The buzz on Christian is that his parents have joint custody, so he'll be spending one semester in Chicago and one semester here.
In Detroit, the buzz is that he's too nice a guy, unwilling to impose draconian job cuts at the risk of angering the UAW.

s.def: To make a low, continuous, humming or sibilant sound, like that made by bees with their wings.
ex: Ah! the singing, fatal arrow, / Like a wasp it buzzed, and stung him [a roebuck]!

s.def: To whisper; to communicate, as tales, in an undertone; to spread, as a report, by whispers or secretly.
ex: I will buzz abroad such prophecies / That Edward shall be fearful of his life.

s.def: To talk to incessantly or confidentially in a low humming voice.
To fly at high speed and at a very low altitude over (an area), as to make a surprise pass.
ex: buzzing around in small cars that dodged through traffic

s.def: A whisper.

ety: From Middle English bosart, from Anglo-Norman buisart, from Old French busart, busard, a derivative ( + -ard) of Old French buison, buson (French buse), possibly from Latin būteō (“hawk”).

s.def: Any of several Old World birds of prey of the genus Buteo with broad wings and a broad tail.
Any scavenging bird, such as the American black vulture (Coragyps atratus) or the turkey vulture (Cathartes aura).
In North America, a curmudgeonly or cantankerous man; an old person; a mean, greedy person.
A blockhead; a dunce.
ex: It is common, to a proverb, to call one who can not be taught, or who continues obstinately ignorant, a buzzard.

s.def: Synonym of double bogey.
A fighter plane.
The insignia of a colonel, or a petty officer within the navy.
A military discharge (due to the military discharge certificate).
A bastard.

ety: Etymology tree English buzz Proto-Indo-European *-yósder. Proto-Italic *-āzios Latin -āriusnom. Latin -āriusbor. Proto-Germanic *-ārijaz Proto-West Germanic *-ārī Old English -ere Middle English -ere English -er English buzzer From buzz + -er.

s.def: One who, or that which, buzzes; an insect that buzzes.
ex: And wants not buzzers to infect his ear / With pestilent speeches of his father's death.

s.def: A device that makes a buzzing sound.
ex: If you think you know the answer to the question, hit the buzzer as fast as you can.

s.def: A police badge.
ex: I flipped my wallet open on her desk and let her look at the buzzer pinned to the flap.

s.def: A run scored from an overthrow.
A pickpocket.
ex: The pickpocket was a Buzzer. The man who booked a room at a hotel, and went round the rooms of other guests, was a Snoozer.
[…] a 'buzzer', for whom picking pockets was an art […]
You can't do the street stuff for ever, you lose your dexterity. I was the oldest and I was trained up for a buzzer — a street thief […]

s.def: A gossip.

ety: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *h₁ep-der. Proto-Indo-European *h₁épsder. Proto-Indo-European *h₁épider. Proto-Indo-European *h₁pi Proto-Germanic *bi Proto-West Germanic *bī Old English bī Middle English by English by From Middle English by, bi, from Old English bī (“by; near; around”), from Proto-West Germanic *bī, from Proto-Germanic *bi (“near; by; around; about”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₁epi. Cognate with West Frisian by (“by; near”), Afrikaans by (“at; by; near”), Saterland Frisian…

s.def: Indicates the person or thing that does or causes something: Through the action or presence of.
ex: The matter was decided by the chairman.
The boat was swamped by the water.
He was protected by his body armour.

s.def: Indicates the creator of a work: Existing through the authorship etc. of.
ex: There are many well-known plays by William Shakespeare

s.def: Indicates a means of achieving something: Involving/using the means of.
ex: I'd know you anywhere by your gravelly voice.
I avoided the guards by moving only when they weren't looking.
By Pythagoras' theorem, we can calculate the length of the hypotenuse.

s.def: Near or next to.
ex: The mailbox is by the bus stop.

s.def: From one side of something to the other, passing close by; past.
ex: The stream runs by our back door.
He ran straight by me.

s.def: Not later than (the given time); not later than the end of (the given time interval); before.
ex: Be back by ten o'clock!
We'll find someone by the end of March.
I'll have been cycling for longer than two hours by lunchtime.

s.def: After a given amount of time has elapsed or a given event has occurred.
ex: By February, we were all sick of the cold.
By the time I realized I had left my phone at home, I was already two blocks from work.
By 29, my financial situation wasn’t just disorganized, it was untenable.

s.def: Indicates an authority according to which something is done.
ex: By the power vested in me, I now pronounce you man and wife.
I live by my own code of ethics.

s.def: Indicates a means of classification or organisation.
ex: I sorted the items by category.
Table 1 shows details of our employees broken down by sex and age.

s.def: Indicates the amount of change, difference or discrepancy
ex: Our stock is up by ten percent.
We won by six goals to three.
His date of birth was wrong by ten years.

s.def: Emphatically yes; certainly; definitely.
ex: By all means take as much salt as you need: that's what neighbors are for.
Each, in its own way, was unforgettable. It would be difficult to… Rome! By all means, Rome. I will cherish my visit here in memory as long as I live.

s.def: Used other than figuratively or idiomatically: see by, all, means.
ex: He vowed to attack her by all means possible, suggesting their war was only just beginning.

ety: From Middle English by and by (“side by side, close together, alongside, on and on, continually, again and again, repeatedly”), equivalent to by + and + by.

s.def: After a short time.
ex: Two anons and a by and by is an hour and a half.

s.def: After an indefinite period.
ex: Sit down, have a rest, and by and by you'll be feeling better.
She said herself She would forgive him, by and by, not now — For her own sake then, if not for mine — not now —- But by and by.
Will the circle be unbroken by and by, by and by? Is a better home awaiting in the sky, in the sky?

s.def: Immediately; at once.
ex: When […] persecution ariseth because of the word, by and by he is offended.

s.def: Heaven; the hereafter. Usually preceded with "the sweet."
ex: I'm sorry ma'am, but your cat's gone on to the sweet by and by.
In the sweet by and by We shall meet on that beautiful shore.

s.def: Unexpectedly, accidentally; without foreplanning.
ex: I stumbled across the exit by chance.

s.def: Possibly; perhaps.
ex: Are you by chance looking for the exit?
If by chance you notice the fine, almost sweet maltiness of the aroma, and the brisk, dry, mineral quality of the flavors, even better.

s.def: During the day.
ex: He is a policeman by day and a thief by night.

s.def: In absence of any opposing action.
ex: If we don't do something, they'll win by default.
No one could think of a better name, so we chose "Strawman" by default.
If he wins an election, it will only be by default.

s.def: To a considerably large extent, easily.
ex: Paris is by far the largest city in France.
These are by far the most impressive narrow-gauge engines in Greece.
Wouldn't it be nobler by far to fight the good fight with all the weapons available: a firm bass voice, a wagging finger, the Bible?

ety: Ellipsis of a full oath of the form "I swear by God that …".

s.def: Used as an oath to emphasize the veracity of an associated statement.
Used as an intensifier.
Manually; without the use of automation or machines.
ex: The computers went down and they had to do all the bookkeeping by hand that day.
A full set costs $245 and takes around 10 to 14 days to make by hand.

s.def: Without suckling it.
ex: to bring up an infant by hand

ety: From Middle English by herte. Compare French par cœur (literally “by heart”), of which the English may be a calque.

s.def: From unaided memory and in full detail.
ex: to learn something by heart
to know something by heart
He used to live in that town, and he still knows all the streets by heart.

s.def: By using (an object or an approach).
ex: Some stone was being loaded into standard gauge wagons by means of a portable conveyor belt.

ety: From by + no + means (“condition or instrument to achieve a result”).

s.def: Certainly not; definitely not; not at all.
ex: By no means am I suggesting that euthanasia should be outlawed, but rather that we should look at its inherent risks.
Is that all you’ve got to say? ―By no means. Let me explain further.

s.def: Alone, without another's immediate company.
ex: She sat by herself in the corner, waiting quietly.

s.def: Unaided; without assistance or help from others.
ex: I have always wondered why shoe salesmen think I can't tie my shoes by myself.
You ate the whole thing by yourself?

s.def: Used other than figuratively or idiomatically: see by, oneself.
ex: He kept the gun by himself at all times.

ety: First appeared in the 10th century with literal meaning "by the side of the road", from Old English weġ (which became "way") meaning "road". Soon afterward (circa 1000) it came to mean "during one's journey". The figurative meaning developed in the mid-16th century, with the first instance of the modern meaning being from 1614.

s.def: Incidentally; used in referencing a parenthetical statement not timely, central, or crucial to the topic at hand; foregone, passed by, something that has already happened.
ex: His mother will be coming for dinner tomorrow, and, by the way, she recently sold her collection of ceramic eggs.
[…] I had counted on a life-lease of the profits, whereas I only received those of a few short years. But this is by the way.

ety: From by- (“side, secondary, ancillary”) + election.

s.def: An election held to fill a political office that has become vacant between general elections.
ex: Coordinate term: general election
In 2015, he was selected as candidate for that year's by-election for the Oldham West and Royton seat. He won with 62% of the vote.
The ANC has accused the IFP of bussing in voters from other wards to vote during the recent Newcastle Municipality by-election won by the IFP.

s.def: Alternative spelling of byline.

ety: From by- + pass.

s.def: Alternative form of bypass.
ex: the Colnbrook By-Pass on the A4

s.def: A consequence, especially a side effect.
ex: The many Indian restaurants all over Britain are a by-product of the large waves of immigration from the subcontinent.

s.def: secondary product
Something made incidentally during the production of something else.

ety: Borrowed from Latin Byblos, from Ancient Greek Βύβλος (Búblos), from Phoenician 𐤂𐤁𐤋 (gbl /⁠Gebal⁠/). Doublet of Jubail.

s.def: A port city in Keserwan-Jbeil Governorate, Lebanon.

ety: Unadapted borrowing from Polish Bydgoszcz.

s.def: The capital and largest city of Kuyavian-Pomeranian Voivodeship, Poland.

s.def: short for goodbye — see also goodbye
Goodbye.
An exclamation of disbelief or dismissal.
ex: Rowlings-Blake responded: "Girl bye, if he can't take criticism from 'a joke', what's he gonna do when somebody real comes for him? #notready"
Her jeans don't even got the loops for her damn belt LMFAO bye 😭

s.def: Goodbye.
ex: Bye bye! Let's play again some time!

s.def: A goodbye.
Bedtime for a toddler, going to sleep, going to bed.
ex: Brush your teeth, it's time to go bye-bye.
"[H]e came to the gate of the city; and finding it shut lay him down and went to by-by!"

s.def: Byelorussian Soviet Socialist Republic, the name for Bolshevik Belarus which became a constituent republic of the Soviet Union (1919–1991), member of the United Nations since 1945.

ety: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *h₁ep-der. Proto-Indo-European *h₁épsder. Proto-Indo-European *h₁épider. Proto-Indo-European *h₁pi Proto-Germanic *bi Proto-West Germanic *bī Old English bī Middle English by English by English gone English bygone From by (adverb) + gone. See go by.

s.def: Having been or happened in the distant past.
An event that happened in the past.
An object from the past; a relic, antique, etc.

ety: From Middle English bylawe, bilawe, partly from Old English bīlage (“bylaw”) and partly from a variant of Middle English byrelawe, birlawe, from Old Norse býjar (“town's; settlement's”) + lǫg (“laws; jurisdiction”). Byrlaw is attested earlier in English but is unattested in Old Norse and the cognates in Scandinavian languages follow the development of bylaw: Danish bylov (“municipal law”), Swedish bylag and byalag.

s.def: A local custom or law of a settlement or district.
A rule made by a local authority to regulate its own affairs.
A law or rule governing the internal affairs of an organization (e.g., corporation or business).

ety: Inherited from Middle English bypath; by surface analysis, by + path.

s.def: An unfrequented path; an indirect route; a byway.

s.def: Alternative form of by-product.

ety: From Middle English bire, bier, byr, from Old English bȳre.

s.def: A barn, especially one used for keeping cattle in.
ex: It was here in the kitchen, in the passage, In the mews in the harn in the byre in the market-place [...]
The visitors came up the narrow road through the forest from the south; they filled the spare-rooms, they bunked out in cow byres and barns.

ety: From Latin byssus, from Ancient Greek βύσσος (bússos, “flax; flax cotton”), from a Semitic source cognate to Hebrew בּוּץ (būṣ, “byssus”) and Aramaic בּוּצָא (būṣā, “byssus”)

s.def: The long fine silky filaments excreted by several mollusks (particularly Pinna nobilis) by which they attach themselves to the sea bed, and from which sea silk is manufactured.
Sea silk manufactured from these filaments.
The stipe or stem of some fungi which are particularly thin and thread-like.

ety: From by- + stander. Compare passerby.

s.def: A person who, although present at some event, does not take part in it; an observer, witness, or spectator.
A social phenomenon where individuals are less likely to offer assistance to a victim when other people are present.

ety: An alteration of the word bite so it would not be accidentally misspelled as bit. Coined by Werner Buchholz in 1956, during the early design phase for the IBM 7030 Stretch computer.

s.def: 8-bit unit
A short sequence of bits (binary digits) that can be operated on as a unit by a computer; the smallest usable machine word.
A unit of computing storage equal to eight bits, which can represent any of 256 distinct values.
ex: The word “hello” fits into five bytes of ASCII code.

ety: From Middle English bywey, equivalent to by- + way.

s.def: A road or track not following a main route; a secondary or minor road or path.
ex: Near-synonyms: back road, back street, back lane

s.def: A road that is not frequently travelled.
a little-known or arcane field of study or detail.

ety: From Middle English byword, byworde (“proverb”), from Old English bīword, bīwyrd, bīwyrde (“proverb, household word", also "adverb”), from Proto-West Germanic *bīwurdī, equivalent to by- + word. Compare Latin proverbium, which byword may possibly be a translation of. Cognate with Old High German pīwurti (“proverb”). Compare also Old English bīspel (“proverb, example”), bīcwide (“byword, proverb, tale, fable”), Dutch bijwoord (“adverb”).

s.def: A proverb or proverbial expression, common saying; a frequently used word or phrase.
A characteristic word or expression; a word or phrase associated with a person or group.
Someone or something that stands as an example (i.e. metonymically) for something else, by having some of that something's characteristic traits.
An object of notoriety or contempt, scorn or derision.
ex: "I know you and Harry are inseparable. Surely for that reason, if for none other, you should not have made his sister's name a by-word."

s.def: A nickname or epithet.
Alternative letter-case form of Byzantine (figurative senses only).
A byzant (coin).

s.def: Of or pertaining to Byzantium.

Belonging to the civilization of the Eastern Roman Empire between 331, when its capital was moved to Constantinople, and 1453, when that capital was conquered by the Turks and ultimately renamed Istanbul.
Overly complex or intricate, especially of bureaucracy.
ex: a Byzantine system of regulations
The byzantine, meandering processes of Icann are engineered in a way that avoids any dissent surfacing, all under the reassuring guise of consensus.

s.def: Of a style of architecture prevalent in the Eastern Empire down to 1453, marked by the round arch springing from columns or piers, the dome supported upon pendentives, capitals elaborately sculptured, mosaic or other encrustations, etc.
Rigid, unceasing, inflexible.
Devious and stealthy.
Of or relating to the Byzantine Rite or any of the many Eastern Orthodox churches and Greek Catholic churches that use this rite for their liturgical celebrations.
A native of Byzantium (modern-day Istanbul) or of the Byzantine empire
Alternative form of byzantine (coin)
A dark, metallic shade of violet.

ety: Calque of Latin Imperium Byzantinum.

s.def: An ancient Greek empire in Southeastern Europe and Western Asia; the predominantly Greek-speaking continuation of the Roman Empire during Late Antiquity and the Middle Ages with its capital at Constantinople (modern-day Istanbul), originally known as Byzantium, which fell in 1453.

Collectively, the continuum of forms of the Greek language as written and spoken during the time of the Byzantine Empire (C.E. 330–1453), preceded by Koine Greek and Early Medieval Greek and succeeded by Late Medieval Greek to Modern Greek. (ISO 639-3 code: grc shared with Classical Greek.)

ety: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *bʰuǵ-der. Thracian *būzasder. Ancient Greek Βῡ́ζᾱς (Bū́zās) Proto-Indo-European *-yósder. Ancient Greek -ῐος (-ĭos)? Ancient Greek -ῐον (-ĭon) Ancient Greek Βῡζᾰ́ντῐον (Būzắntĭon)bor. Latin Bȳzantiumbor. English Byzantium From Latin Bȳzantium, from Ancient Greek Βῡζᾰ́ντῐον (Būzắntĭon), named after its legendary founder, Byzas.

s.def: An ancient Greek city situated on the Bosporus in modern Turkey, renamed Constantinople in 330 C.E.; modern Istanbul.
An ancient Greek empire in Southeastern Europe and Western Asia, with its capital at Constantinople; in full, Byzantine Empire.

ety: Imitative. Compare buzz.

s.def: The buzzing sound of a bee, wasp, etc.
